If she’s hung up on the idea of you “proving” yourself in some way, remind her that real strength isn’t about throwing punches—it’s about making smart decisions, even when they’re hard.

What advice changed your life financially? The best piece of financial advice I ever received was simple yet profound: “Spend less than you earn.” It sounds almost laughably obvious, but when I first heard it, I was drowning in credit card debt, living paycheck to paycheck, and constantly justifying my impulsive purchases with the mantra of “I deserve this.” My mentor, an older colleague who had retired comfortably in his early 50s, noticed my financial chaos and pulled me aside one day. He didn’t lecture me or shame me; instead, he asked me to sit down with him and lay out my monthly income and expenses. Seeing it all written down was eye-opening. I was spending nearly 20% of my income on things I didn’t need—takeout meals, subscription services I barely used, and random online purchases that seemed harmless at the time but added up quickly. He told me to start small: cut one unnecessary expense and put that money into savings instead. That first step felt insignificant, but over time, it grew into a habit. I began tracking every dollar, setting a budget, and prioritizing needs over wants. It wasn’t glamorous, and there were days when I felt deprived, but the peace of mind that came from having a financial cushion was worth it. Within a year, I had paid off my credit card debt and started building an emergency fund. It wasn’t about deprivation or extreme frugality; it was about making intentional choices and understanding the difference between a short-term thrill and long-term stability. That advice didn’t just change my bank account; it changed my mindset. I stopped seeing money as something to be spent immediately and started seeing it as a tool to build the life I wanted. To this day, I live by that principle, and it’s allowed me to weather financial storms without panic, pursue opportunities I wouldn’t have been able to before, and even help others who are struggling with their own finances.

What has an employee said that immediately caused you to fire them? I once had an employee who, during a team meeting, made a snide comment about how the company’s policies were “designed to keep people like them down.” At first, I thought it was just frustration, but then they doubled down by saying, “Honestly, this place is a joke, and I’m only here because I need the paycheck.” To make matters worse, they turned to a colleague and muttered, “You’re too good for this, you should quit too.” It wasn’t just the disrespect toward the company or me—it was the deliberate attempt to undermine morale and encourage others to leave. In that moment, it was clear they had no intention of contributing positively to the team or the workplace culture. I pulled them aside after the meeting and let them go. I’ve always believed in giving people chances, but there’s a line where negativity becomes toxic, and they crossed it. It’s one thing to voice concerns constructively; it’s another to actively sow discord. The irony is that they were a decent worker when they applied themselves, but their attitude made it impossible to keep them on. Looking back, I don’t regret the decision. A workplace thrives on mutual respect and effort, and anyone who undermines that doesn’t deserve a spot on the team.

What movies do you like but everybody hates, and why? Ah, the cinematic pariahs—those films that everyone seems to loathe but you secretly cherish. For me, it’s *Battlefield Earth* (2000). Yes, the one with John Travolta and the alien Psychlos. The consensus is that it’s a disaster, a cinematic black hole of cornball dialogue, over-the-top performances, and perplexing camera angles. But here’s the thing: I find it gloriously absurd. It’s like watching a B-movie on steroids, a film so earnest in its ridiculousness that it transcends its flaws. Travolta’s cackling villainy, the hilariously convoluted plot about humans overthrowing their alien overlords using 1,000-year-old fighter jets—it’s all so unintentionally entertaining. It’s the kind of movie that feels like it was made by aliens who had only a vague understanding of human storytelling. And the cherry on top? The Psychlos’ obsession with gold, which is explained with the profound insight: “It’s valuable because it’s rare.” Yes, thank you, movie. Earth-shattering wisdom.    Another one I’ll defend is *The Room* (2003). It’s not so much a “so bad it’s good” film as it is a surrealist masterpiece. The dialogue, the acting, the inexplicable football tossing—every frame feels like it belongs to a parallel universe where logic and coherence are optional. Tommy Wiseau’s performance as Johnny is a study in baffling sincerity, and the film’s utter lack of self-awareness makes it endlessly fascinating. It’s like watching a car crash in slow motion, except the car is made of pure, unfiltered weirdness.    Then there’s *Catwoman* (2004). Halle Berry’s portrayal of the feline antihero is often ridiculed, and the basketball scene is, admittedly, one of the most bizarre moments in superhero cinema. But I can’t help but admire its audacity. It’s a film that dares to be different, even if “different” means nonsensical. The way it leans into its campiness, the over-the-top action sequences, the bizarre cat metaphors—it’s a trainwreck, but it’s *my* trainwreck.    So, yes, these films are flawed, often hilariously so. But that’s precisely why I love them. They’re unapologetically themselves, flaws and all. And isn’t there something oddly endearing about that?

What disturbing rumor turned out to be true at your school? A rumor had been circulating for months that one of the substitute teachers, Mr. Hargrove, wasn’t actually certified to teach. He’d been filling in for various subjects, from math to history, and while some students found his lessons engaging, others noticed glaring inaccuracies. He once claimed the Civil War ended in 1864 and insisted that Pluto was still a planet—classic stuff you’d expect from someone winging it. Still, most of us shrugged it off as just another quirky substitute. But then, during a staff meeting, it was revealed that Mr. Hargrove had never completed his teaching certification. In fact, he’d been hired based on a resume that heavily exaggerated his qualifications. The administration had only discovered the truth after a routine background check flagged inconsistencies. What followed was a swift but quiet dismissal, though not before he’d spent nearly a year molding young minds—or, more accurately, mangling them. The kicker? He’d been collecting a full teacher’s salary the entire time. It’s funny now, in a “how did no one notice this sooner?” kind of way, but at the time, it left us questioning just how thorough the hiring process really was. Rumors like these always carry a hint of “that can’t possibly be true,” but every so often, they’re validated in the most unsettling ways. It’s a reminder that sometimes, the stories whispered in hallways aren’t just tall tales—they’re warnings.

Which TV shows were popular when you were younger that would flop today? Why? Growing up in the late ’90s and early 2000s, TV was a wild, unfiltered landscape where shows could get away with just about anything. Remember *Married… with Children*? That show was a cornerstone of cable television, but if it aired today, it would be torn to shreds by social media within hours. Al Bundy’s misogynistic rants, Peggy’s laziness, and Kelly’s ditzy persona would be labeled as toxic stereotypes faster than you could say “No Ma’am.” And let’s not even get started on the *Jerry Springer Show*. That chaos-fueled circus of human dysfunction was a guilty pleasure for many, but in today’s climate, it would be condemned for exploiting vulnerable people for entertainment. There’s no way it would survive without cancel culture breathing down its neck.  Then there’s *Friends*, the gold standard of sitcoms back then. Sure, it’s still nostalgic for many, but rewatching it now reveals some glaring issues. The lack of diversity, the fat-shaming jokes aimed at Monica, and the endless gay panic humor from Chandler wouldn’t fly today. And Ross? Oh, Ross. His possessive, whiny behavior would make him the butt of every Twitter thread. Even *Seinfeld*, the self-proclaimed “show about nothing,” would struggle. Its relentless cynicism and borderline sociopathic characters might not resonate as much in an era where audiences crave more nuanced, empathetic storytelling.  Reality TV wasn’t immune either. *The Simple Life*, starring Paris Hilton and Nicole Richie, thrived on the premise of mocking working-class people and rural lifestyles. Today, it would be criticized as tone-deaf and elitist. And let’s not forget *Punk’d*, where Ashton Kutcher relentlessly pranked celebrities. While it was hilarious at the time, the idea of ambushing people with traumatic scenarios for laughs would raise serious ethical concerns now.  Shows like *The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air* and *The Cosby Show* (pre-scandal, of course) might still hold up in terms of humor and heart, but even they’d face scrutiny for their portrayal of certain issues. *The Fresh Prince* tackled serious topics like race and class, but its slapstick humor and exaggerated characters might feel outdated. As for *The Cosby Show*, well, let’s just say it’s a cautionary tale of how a legacy can be irrevocably tainted.  The truth is, TV has evolved, and so have we. What was once funny or entertaining now feels problematic or downright cringeworthy. It’s a reminder that while we can still enjoy these shows for what they were, we’re living in a different world—one that demands more thoughtfulness and responsibility from creators.

The Good, the Bad & the Ugly is an amazing movie but I never understood the scene involving Tuco and his monk brother. As much as it was an emotional scene, it did not advance the movie plot at all. Did Leone ever explain why he added the scene? The scene involving Tuco and his monk brother in *The Good, the Bad & the Ugly* is often debated among fans and critics alike. While it may seem like a narrative detour, some argue that it serves a deeper purpose. Leone, known for his deliberate pacing and attention to character development, likely included it to add layers to Tuco’s otherwise chaotic and self-serving persona. Here’s a man who’s spent most of the movie as a greedy, loud-mouthed outlaw, but in this moment, we see a glimpse of vulnerability and humanity. The interaction with his brother, a man of faith, juxtaposes Tuco’s life of crime with the possibility of redemption—a theme subtly woven throughout the film.  That said, I can see why some viewers find the scene jarring. It doesn’t propel the plot forward in the same way as the treasure hunt or the iconic standoff. It’s more of a character study, a quiet interlude in an otherwise action-packed narrative. Leone was famous for his long, lingering shots and his ability to let moments breathe, but this particular scene feels almost like a short film within the movie. It’s as if Leone wanted to remind us that even in a world of greed and violence, there’s room for introspection and emotional depth.  As for whether Leone ever explained the scene’s inclusion, there’s no definitive answer. He was notoriously tight-lipped about his creative choices, often leaving interpretation up to the audience. Some speculate it was a nod to the Italian neorealist films of the 1940s and 50s, which often explored themes of morality and family. Others believe it was simply Leone indulging in his love for melodrama. Whatever the reason, it’s a scene that lingers, not because it moves the story forward, but because it adds a layer of complexity to Tuco’s character. It’s the kind of detail that makes a rewatch worthwhile, as you notice things you might have missed the first time around. And isn’t that what makes a film truly great? The ability to reveal something new with each viewing?

What should I absolutely not do when visiting your country? Do not, under any circumstances, assume that our local customs are merely quaint suggestions. Yes, you’re a guest, and yes, you’re likely unfamiliar with the nuances, but ignorance is no excuse for outright disrespect. For instance, if you visit a temple, don’t waltz in with your shoes on, snapping photos like you’re at a tourist trap. These places are sacred, not Instagram backdrops. And don’t even think about touching religious artifacts or statues, no matter how “cool” they look or how much you want to prove to your friends back home that you’re “cultured.” You’re not. You’re just rude.    Another cardinal sin: don’t complain about the food. If you’re offered something, even if it looks like it might bite you back, you eat it with a smile and a thank you. Making a face or asking, “What is this?” is a surefire way to earn the eternal disdain of your hosts. And for the love of all that’s sensible, don’t compare it to the “authentic” version you had at some fusion restaurant in your hometown. It’s not the same, and you’re not a food critic.    Lastly, don’t be that person who bargains aggressively in local markets, treating every transaction like a battlefield. Sure, haggling is expected in some places, but there’s a line between negotiation and exploitation. If you’re haggling over a dollar like it’s the last one you’ll ever see, maybe reconsider your priorities. Remember, what’s a trivial amount to you might be a significant portion of someone’s livelihood.    And one more thing—don’t litter. Ever. It doesn’t matter if you’re in a remote village or a bustling city, throwing trash on the ground is the height of arrogance. If you can’t find a bin, hold onto it until you do. You’re not leaving a “mark” on the country; you’re just proving you don’t deserve to be there.    So, to sum it up: don’t disrespect our culture, don’t insult our food, don’t exploit our markets, and don’t trash our streets. If you can manage that, you’ll find that the people here are among the most welcoming in the world. But if you can’t, don’t be surprised if you’re met with side-eyes, muttered curses, and possibly a swift escort out of certain places. You’ve been warned.
